belief: I can't be happy as long as I hurt.
origins: Pain narrows attention, and joy can seem like something that belongs to healthy people. We may stop doing what we enjoy and give up on laughter, connection, and meaning until the pain is gone.
teaches: Paul wrote, “I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances,” and described himself as “Sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10). The psalmist says, “When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul” (Psalm 94:19). Joy is not the absence of pain. It is a gift that can exist beside pain, in small and real moments, and in the nearness of God.
self_statements: Happiness is impossible while I hurt.
I do not deserve to enjoy anything.
I will be happy when the pain stops.
errors: Believing I am either pain-free and happy or miserable.
Predicting that I cannot enjoy anything.
Feeling pain and concluding joy is impossible.
Calling myself unable to enjoy life.
questions: When have I felt a moment of peace or joy despite pain?
What small pleasures are still possible?
What did Paul and the psalmists experience in suffering?
Whom do I enjoy being with?
What would I tell a friend who felt this way?
What gentle joy can I plan this week?
truth: Joy and pain can exist together. I can look for small gifts each day, receive God’s consolation, and enjoy what I can, without waiting for the pain to end.
hw_truths: I can be sorrowful yet rejoicing.
Joy is found in His presence.
I can enjoy what I can.
log: Each day, name one moment of joy or peace.
actions: Write simple things you can still enjoy.
prayer: Lord, pain has taken my joy. Give me Your consolation, help me notice small gifts, and let me enjoy what I can. Amen.
